contentBlocks.text: by Todd Friedman | Sep 5, 2026 | 1990s , 2000s , Reviews

There are some arcade games that simply don’t need much introduction. ARKANOID is one of them. Originally released by Taito in 1986, the paddle-and-ball classic became one of the defining block-breaking games of the arcade era. Its 1987 sequel, ARKANOID: REVENGE OF DOH , took the basic formula and expanded it with new enemies, stage designs, power-ups, and challenges.

Now HAMSTER Corporation has brought ARKANOID: REVENGE OF DOH to Nintendo Switch 2 as part of its Arcade Archives 2 series. Rather than completely remake the game for modern audiences, HAMSTER takes a preservation-first approach, keeping the original arcade experience intact while adding modern features that make the game considerably more convenient to play today.
The result is one of those releases that understands exactly what makes an old arcade game special.
the ball, and advance through increasingly difficult stages.
The sequel adds considerably more variety to that formula. Blocks can move, regenerate, or behave differently, while enemies and obstacles make later stages much more challenging.
There is also a branching stage structure, allowing players to take different routes through the game.
Arcade Archives 2 Features
This is where HAMSTER’s Switch 2 release becomes more than simply playing an old game on new hardware.
The release includes several different ways to play, including Original Mode, Hi Score Mode, Caravan Mode, and Time Attack Mode.
Time Attack is particularly interesting because it changes the objective. Instead of concentrating exclusively on score, you’re trying to complete the game as quickly as possible.
There are also save features, online rankings, rewind functionality, and rapid-fire options.
These additions don’t fundamentally change REVENGE OF DOH . Instead, they give modern players different ways to enjoy the original game.
That is exactly the approach I want to see from a classic-game collection.
At around the $10 price point, this is an easy recommendation for classic arcade fans.
The value proposition is somewhat different for players who aren’t interested in arcade history.
You’re essentially buying a faithful recreation of a game that is nearly four decades old, rather than a brand-new Switch 2 production.
But for players who appreciate classic arcade gaming, that’s precisely the appeal.
HAMSTER has preserved the original game while adding features that make it considerably easier to enjoy on modern hardware.

h1: Atari and Vice Beer Introduce New Beer Collection

contentBlocks.text: by Old School Gamer | Sep 5, 2026 | 1980s , 1990s , Press Release
ATARI AND VICE BEER INTRODUCE NEW BEER COLLECTION
The four-pack of Atari-themed beer is available now.

September 5, 2026 – Atari and Vice Beer are celebrating a new licensing collaboration during PAX West in Seattle. Vancouver, Washington-based Vice Beer has released a four-pack of Atari-themed 16 oz. beers, including One-Button Joystick WC IPA, Gemstone Sour, Sunken Treasure and Original Bug Battle Hazy IPA. The four-packs can be purchased online via atari.com or at shop.tavour.com .

“I remember the thrill of walking into an arcade with a pocket full of quarters, and that is how I feel sharing these hand-crafted, Atari-themed beers with fans,” said Michael Perozzo, co-founder of Vice Beer. “There is something for everyone in this collection, and the artwork is satisfyingly retro.”
The four-beer collection includes:

One-Button Joystick – 1x 16oz can – WCIPA – 6.9% ABV Featuring the absolutely iconic controller of the Atari 2600, Vice and Atari opted for a suitable craft classic for One-Button Joystick — a West Coast IPA. The crushable Westie starts with a Pilsner malt base for a crisp sip that’ll keep you quenched as you blast asteroid after asteroid. It is hopped with Columbus Cryo, Strata, Idaho 7, Citra, Mosaic Cryo, and Quantum Mosaic, culminating in a sip as mind blowing as being able to play Asteroids … in your house! Which in the ‘80s was pretty exciting!

Expect bright mango and grapefruit to lead each dynamic swig with hints of tropical fruit and mixed berry flowing underneath. Nuances of orange peel and piney resin should bring a refreshing balance that’ll have you diving back in for another sip like you’re trying to set a high score!

Original Bug Battle – 1x 16oz can – NEIPA – 6.4% ABV Look for luscious mandarin and peach to weave like a Centipede through notes of pineapple and strawberry on every pillowy swig. Zesty lime and white grape tones ought to crawl underneath with just enough peppery bitterness on the finish to balance all that nectar.

To craft this IPA, the team brewed a soft base with Pilsner malt, flaked oat, and torrified wheat. Then they blasted it with Nelson, Motueka, Strata, Citra Cryo, Mosaic Cryo, and Quantum Galaxy for surges of straight nectar. It all makes for Haze so satisfying, you’ll be after every last drop like they’re segments of a centipede that need destroying!

Gemstone Sour – 1x 16oz can – Fruited Sour – 5% ABV Like Bentley Bear working his way through colorful fortresses in search of gems in the arcade classic Crystal Castles, you’ll find yourself happily lost in a maze of jammy bramble fruit and succulent citrus with every swig of this Sour. Imagine an extra tangy take on a berry lemonade and you have a decent idea what’s in store!
This gem is brewed with castle-sized quantities of actual raspberries and lemons. Paired with a tart Sour Ale base, it makes for an invigorating swig that’ll keep you going game after game!

Sunken Treasure – 1x 16oz can – Imperial Stout – 8% ABV For this stunner, Vice teamed up with Nightdive Studios — a game studio and part of the Atari family with an emphasis on retro video game preservation and restoration. That’s fitting, since once you get a taste of this Stout, you’ll probably be looking to preserve every last bit all for yourself!

Especially with all the sumptuous s’mores flavors brimming out of each quaff courtesy of toasted marshmallows, graham crackers, and cacao nibs. Your average campfire treat doesn’t come with delectable espresso tones and hints of caramel from a bold malty base. Oh, and an 8% ABV!

“Nightdive has always been about celebrating the games and experiences that made us fall in love with this medium, and there’s something special about seeing that passion extend beyond the screen,” said Stephen Kick, studio head at Nightdive. “Collaborating with Vice Beer and Atari on Sunken Treasure was a fun way to bring a little piece of that history into the real world. Games are meant to be shared, remembered and enjoyed — and in this case, so is the beer.”

articles.title: Prácticamente magia o El diablo viste de Prada muestran que la nostalgia es el más efectivo de los engaños
articles.description: La nostalgia nos hace creer que queremos pagar para ver segundas partes de películas que nos gustaron en su día, pero al salir del cine nos encontramos con una oscura realidad.

h1: Prácticamente magia o El diablo viste de Prada muestran que la nostalgia es el más efectivo de los engaños

contentBlocks.text: Estamos volviendo al pasado. Aunque, en honor a la verdad, el pasado es algo a lo que no paramos de volver porque nunca lo hemos soltado. La terrible trampa en la que nos hemos visto atrapadas se llama nostalgia. Si bien la nostalgia admite muchas formas y no se presenta de la misma manera para todo el mundo, porque al final es un estado condicionado por demasiados factores personales, la temporalidad acaba siendo un buen punto en común para el público.

Recuerdo cómo la película animada Red de Pixar pegó muy fuerte en 2022 porque nos hizo darnos cuenta de algo: La nostalgia de los 2020 ya no tiene que beber de manera necesaria de los años 80 porque la gente que creció en los 2000 es ahora mayor y empieza a recordar el pasado con ese cariño melancólico idéntico al que ha empujado a Hollywood durante décadas a rescatar el imaginario audiovisual de Steven Spielberg en sus largometrajes del siglo anterior.

Y, por eso mismo, este año hemos sido testigos de cómo han vuelto a las salas películas como Prácticamente magia (1998) o El diablo viste de Prada (2006) con sus respectivas secuelas un cuarto de lustro después. No es casualidad. Ahora es un buen momento para regresar a ellas, para atraer a una nueva generación a los cines.

Porque, y este es el elemento más importante del fenómeno, la nostalgia vende. ¿Segundas partes nunca fueron buenas? Si la primera te gustó, lo más seguro es que quieras ir a ver la segunda. No le vas a poner muchas pegas, te va a dar lo mismo de lo que trate, quién actué.

Tú conoces la base, el origen, y eso es lo único que te va a importar a la hora de lanzarte a pagar una entrada. Y, aun así, hay un giro en este juego del que todavía no eres consciente, pero que se te va a ir desvelando a medida que aceptes el engaño de la productora que quiso traer de vuelta tu querida película de los 2000.

En su día viste aquella cinta y tenía algo que te conquistó. Se quedó grabada en tu memoria, o perdida entre el resto de tus recuerdos, pero formó parte de tu vida en algún momento que fue mejor, porque el presente siempre empora frente a lo que proyectamos sobre lo que ya pasó.

Por eso, cuando anuncian una secuela algo se despierta en tu interior: la nostalgia. Ha pasado el tiempo, ¡cuanto más mejor! De repente tienes la genuina necesidad de querer saber qué pasó después: cómo habrá envejecido esa trama, qué más se podrá contar de esos personajes, ¿habrán evolucionado o se habrán estancado después de todos estos años?

La respuesta la tienes en dos nuevas horas de película que llegan para saciar tu FOMO por estas tres décadas olvidadas... Tan solo para que te des cuenta de que, al final, te acabas quedando con la primera cuando ya has pagado por la segunda. Y es que ha transcurrido demasiado tiempo desde que se lanzó la original.

Tú ya no eres esa chavala que en su día fue al cine a ver Prácticamente magia o El diablo viste de Prada, ahora eres una señora. Sí, te lo has pasado bien viendo la segunda parte, has recordado con cariño aquello que te gustaba entonces. Pero su historia nunca estará a la altura de la película que ya habías construido en tu cabeza sobre su posible retorno.

Eso que te hizo gracia hace 20 años o esas dinámicas que te llamaron la atención carecen de la chispa de la originalidad de entonces. Ahora ya no te gusta lo que te gustaba en aquel momento, su historia se siente como rescatar un barco que debía permanecer hundido para no corromperse fuera del océano que lo consumió.

La nostalgia te llama con una fuerza poderosa para que vuelvas a esos universos que conociste cuando todo era diferente, sin que esperes la decepción de encontrarte con que todo lo que te atraía de la secuela era lo que iba a hacer que no funcionase el reencuentro.
A veces es mejor no remover el pasado, dejarlo todo como está y recordarlo con cariño sin forzar su vuelta.

articles.description: 🤝 Don't want to see ads? Become a premium member for $3 a month and support an independent publication today! A couple of days ago, Sony & LEGO announced the PlayStation set , featuring 1,911 bricks, releasing on October 4th and priced at £139.99/$179.99.

images.caption: An Emulation Mod Kit For The LEGO PlayStation Is In The Works

h1: An Emulation Mod Kit For The LEGO PlayStation Is In The Works

contentBlocks.text: A couple of days ago, Sony & LEGO announced the PlayStation set , featuring 1,911 bricks, releasing on October 4th and priced at £139.99/$179.99. It has gone down very well with most retro gamers (let's not talk about how it doesn't have 1,995 pieces), featuring two secret easter eggs on the inside which can be pulled out to display Ape Escape and Gran Turismo dioramas.

The LEGO set isn't out yet, but there's already something special in the works for this build: a mod kit from the makers of the BrickBoy . This kit will turn the LEGO PlayStation into a working games console thanks to an inserted Raspberry Pi Zero 2W offering PS1 Emulation, HDMI out and more.

The BrickBoy was an incredibly innovative piece of tech that transformed the GAME BOY into a working console that you built yourself; everything the team from Switzerland has learned from that first project is now going into developing a more advanced mod kit for the LEGO PlayStation, being named the BrickStation .

I spoke with the founder of BrickStation, Thomas Bertani, to get a better understanding of their upcoming product. It's clear that it's still in very early development; heck, they don't have the set yet, but they know exactly what they want to do, and how they're going to do it, so let me explain.

The components of the BrickStation will be assembled inside of an ABS, mould-injected "base"; this will contain the Raspberry Pi and all of the electronics, crammed into a build small enough to fit into the exact compartment that the Ape Escape diorama sits, allowing you to hopefully slide it into the console easily, perhaps not removing any bricks or pieces at all. Thomas said he wants this to be as close to "plug and play" as possible.

The Raspberry Pi internals will offer easy hook-up to an HDMI TV, offer wireless controller support, wired controller support via USB, the ability to use the Power On button on the LEGO PS1 and a "full-resolution, full-frame-rate" gaming experience. Thomas mentioned there will also be full compliance with regulations and certifications, which isn't something fan-made mod kits do, and can be dangerous, so it's clear Thomas and his team want this to be executed professionally and properly, which their BrickBoy did respectfully.

There's also a number of extra goodies and features that will be announced in the future that we cannot mention. You can follow BrickStation's journey at BrickStation.xyz , and you can likely expect the Kickstarter campaign to launch at the end of the month or around the official release of the LEGO set. As of now, we have no information regarding pricing or release date, but we're confident these guys will pull it off and no doubt they'll have a bunch of extra features and products to explore once the crowdfunding campaign goes live. We'll try our hardest to give you an early look at this, just like we did with the BrickBoy, so make sure to follow our free weekly newsletter to not miss out on that.

contentBlocks.text: This is the year of awesome frontends. Independent developers, handheld enthusiasts, and app makers are all building something cool in the space. It was only recently that I finished writing about Socket , a frontend focusing on cartridge/disc art, and it was only a couple of days ago when I showcased DigitBitPlay , another frontend focusing on the physical side of digital retro games.

Now, a well-known retro-gaming YouTuber known as Ryan Retro has spent the last few months developing his very own Android frontend for emulators, again with a focus on the physical aspect of digital collecting. This seems to be a trend after Sony's big announcement of stopping the production of physical games.

Ryan is calling this frontend "Jump", conveniently named because of the application's ease of jumping to certain games in your collection. Ryan wants it to be a simple yet effective way to organise your ROM library using its box art, allowing you to resize, readjust and move around the collection in a way that's natural to you; heck, you even choose case view, which makes your cartridges look like they're in an old 2000s storage case surrounded by foam and your discs look like they're in a transparent sleeve.

There's a whole lot of customisations in here that make it easy for you to find a display that suits your needs; you can choose from Grid, Shelf, Tower and Case, and each allows you to change between light and dark themes, even going as far as adding a wooden shelf mode too, to keep things nostalgic. These views are kept when searching for your games using the keyboard too.

One of the craziest features though, is the fact that Ryan has built his own scraping service for box art and disc/cartidge art, so you don't have to pair this with any external app or service such as ScreenScraper, you literally press "download it for me" and Jump will automatically find, download and update your ROM library with box art images and cartridge/disc art so that your collection is organised visually straight after installing it. That's incredible, and kudos to Ryan for making it incredibly fluid. Just make sure your ROM files are named exactly the same as the game title for this to work smoothly.

You can also add multiple folders to a specific console, which is not typical of frontends, allowing you to take advantage of the internal and external storage at the same time. This syncs up your entire library wherever it may be. It works with an array of Android-based retro handhelds, and even dual-screen ones too such as the AYN Thor.

This frontend is locked behind a Patreon paywall , which is typical of indie-made frontends these days, so to get hold of it you'll have to throw Ryan a few bucks to get access to this frontend on Android. You'll also get updates and newer updates as the months go on without having to keep paying, so $3 will get you this app and its continued updates, which is awesome.

The ShockLine range is out right now, with both charging cable kits and power supply kits available to purchase. In terms of home consoles, you can purchase:
And in the handhelds range:
Built with flexible, kink-resistant cabling and (on the handheld kits) built-in overcharge protection, so your system stays powered without the wear and tear that comes with old, worn-out originals.

The sets come with the adapters and power supply kits mentioned, as well as a 6-foot USB-C cable so you can place your consoles effectively without having to tower them on top of each other - we've worked with some companies that send the smallest USB cables known to gaming kind with their products, so this is a nice feature.

For power solutions that remove the need for tonnes of bulky wires behind your TV, I think that's a great price, especially because power cords end up getting lost or damaged over the years too. h1: The Interface Details That Made Computer Solitaire Feel Timeless
h2: The Interface Details That Made Computer Solitaire Feel Timeless

contentBlocks.text: The Interface Details That Made Computer Solitaire Feel Timeless
Posted by Retromash
in Misc
Tagged with

Computer solitaire became memorable because it made a new machine feel understandable. A modern round on PlaySolitaire still uses the same essential visual language: a deck, clear columns, visible suits and cards that respond directly to the player. The technology around the game has changed dramatically, but the interaction remains immediate. That is why solitaire belongs in any conversation about the everyday design of classic computer games.

A deck became a lesson in mouse movement When Solitaire arrived with Windows 3.0 in 1990, many home computer users were still becoming comfortable with a mouse. Moving cards from one pile to another gave drag and drop a purpose that was easy to grasp. The player did not need to understand files, menus or commands. They only needed to recognise a card and place it where the rules allowed.

That was clever interface design disguised as a familiar pastime. The action on screen matched an action people already understood from the physical world. A card could be selected, moved and released. If the destination was wrong, the game refused the move. The feedback was simple and immediate.

The desktop game that needed little explanation Many early computer games had to teach players a new language. They introduced unfamiliar controls, icons and objectives at the same time. Solitaire avoided much of that work because the deck already carried meaning.

Red and black suits were easy to distinguish. Ordered columns showed progress. Empty spaces suggested possibility. The stock pile invited a click. Even a player who did not know every rule could experiment and learn from the response.

This made the game unusually approachable. It felt like software, but it did not feel technical. That balance helped it become part of the everyday computer rather than a special activity reserved for dedicated players.

Small interface choices built trust Classic solitaire interfaces were rarely spectacular. Their strength came from consistency. Cards stayed where they were placed. Legal moves behaved predictably. A completed sequence created a visible sense of order.

Those details built trust between the player and the machine. The computer was not hiding the rules or asking for a complicated input. It was maintaining the table, enforcing the structure and keeping score.

The same principle still matters in modern design. A good interface should make the next action feel obvious without making the result automatic. Solitaire achieves this with very little visual clutter. The player can see the problem, but solving it still requires attention.

Nostalgia is visual, but usability keeps it alive The green felt background and pixel card backs are powerful nostalgic images. They recall family computers, office breaks and the particular sound of a mouse button. Yet nostalgia alone does not explain why the game survives.

People return because the underlying interaction remains useful. A round starts quickly. Progress is visible. Failure is understandable. A new attempt creates a different arrangement without requiring a tutorial.

This is also why many attempts to modernise classic games go too far. Extra animations, reward systems and crowded menus can obscure the quality that made the original work. Solitaire does not need to pretend to be bigger than it is. Its modest scale is part of the appeal.

The browser is the new family computer The family computer once gathered software in a single physical place. Today, the browser performs a similar role across laptops, tablets and phones. It provides a common surface where a familiar game can appear without installation or a long setup process.

That shift changes access, but not the core experience. A card still needs a clear destination. A sequence still needs to be read. The player still chooses between an immediate move and a more patient plan.

Browser play also preserves another old habit: using a simple game as a boundary between tasks. One round can mark the end of work, fill a short wait or provide a calm reset before returning to something more demanding.

Why the old rhythm survives Computer solitaire lasts because its rhythm was never tied to one machine. It begins with disorder, asks for careful attention and rewards the gradual creation of structure. The interface supports that rhythm without getting in the way.

That is a useful lesson from classic software. Technology becomes memorable when it gives people a clear action, a reliable response and enough space to make their own decisions. Solitaire did that on the early desktop, and it continues to do it in the browser today.

h1: PlayCase Is A New Retro iPhone Controller With Real Triggers

contentBlocks.text: This is a product I have been following for a long time, and I have even been in discussions with their team regarding review samples, but I'll be completely honest: I still don't know how to feel about this product, and I'll explain why. But I know some of our Retro Dodo readers will find this thing interesting, so I want to put a spotlight on it, seeing as it's now officially available to purchase and I know the owner behind it has been hard at work making this a real thing.

The PlayCase is a new phone case for iPhone (and the Samsung Galaxy S26) that adds physical buttons which pair with a range of emulators such as Delta, RetroArch, and more, similar to the GAMEBABY case that we have reviewed in the past.

What's cool is that the controller part of the case is removable and is stored on the back of the case over the cameras; this can then be snapped off and used on the front of the iPhone as buttons. Keen eyes will also see that this has triggers too, which are located on the back. I am still uncertain how these work because the "learn more" button under the triggers part of the website doesn't work, but I believe it uses rubber bands that wrap around the case internally to activate on-screen presses.

My issue here lies in the manufacturing process. This is 3D printed, and from previous experience, these types of 3D printed products feel scratchy, flakey, are flimsy, and lack strength in the overall build, which is needed in a case that's going to protect a $1,000+ smartphone. However, I have yet to try it in person; this is just something I have experience with, as I own and operate GAMENOOK , a collectable accessory company that manufactures plastic products made from 100% recycled plastic handpressed into aluminium moulds. We tried 3D printing, but it lacked strength and overall quality, and I fear this is the same.

If you don't mind that, and are a fan of 3D-printed products like this, then let me tell you more about this quirky device. The main product is the "PlayCase Case", which surrounds your iPhone; this costs $19.99, and you then pair it with a "Faceplate". You have three to choose from: a "Handheld Faceplate" costing $9.99 that features a DPAD and two action buttons; there's a "Dual Screen Faceplate" that gives you most screen real estate for DS emulation and four action buttons for $14.99; and finally the "Classic Faceplate", also $14.99 and offers four action buttons. So a full kit will cost anywhere between $29.98 and $34.98.

There's also decent repairability with it, which is a great feature and one I completely respect. PlayCase offer all of the small bits and parts to be purchased again for a few bucks should you want to tinker or fix your case in the future; from extra buttons to rubber bands to silicone pads, they'll sort you out should anything go wrong.

It's a fun way to add physical buttons to your device that can be snapped on and off easily. If you're willing to accept that you'll see printing lines and that some areas may lack strength, then this could be one to explore if you're looking for more comfortable emulator controls that include working shoulder buttons. It's certainly in a market of high competition too, seeing as the 8BITDO FlipPad has sold well, the GamesirTaco also, and then there's the GAMEBABY Case that does the same and is mass-produced in high-quality materials, though it has no back buttons.
It's worth noting that there is a sprinkling of Gen-AI amongst the website too, which isn't appreciated by the gaming community.

The PlayCase is a new phone case for iPhone (and the Samsung Galaxy S26) that adds physical buttons which pair with a range of emulators such as Delta, RetroArch, and more, similar to the GAMEBABY case that we have reviewed in the past.

What's cool is that the controller part of the case is removable and is stored on the back of the case over the cameras; this can then be snapped off and used on the front of the iPhone as buttons. Keen eyes will also see that this has triggers too, which are located on the back. I am still uncertain how these work because the "learn more" button under the triggers part of the website doesn't work, but I believe it uses rubber bands that wrap around the case internally to activate on-screen presses.

My issue here lies in the manufacturing process. This is 3D printed, and from previous experience, these types of 3D printed products feel scratchy, flakey, are flimsy, and lack strength in the overall build, which is needed in a case that's going to protect a $1,000+ smartphone. However, I have yet to try it in person; this is just something I have experience with, as I own and operate GAMENOOK , a collectable accessory company that manufactures plastic products made from 100% recycled plastic handpressed into aluminium moulds. We tried 3D printing, but it lacked strength and overall quality, and I fear this is the same.

If you don't mind that, and are a fan of 3D-printed products like this, then let me tell you more about this quirky device. The main product is the "PlayCase Case", which surrounds your iPhone; this costs $19.99, and you then pair it with a "Faceplate". You have three to choose from: a "Handheld Faceplate" costing $9.99 that features a DPAD and two action buttons; there's a "Dual Screen Faceplate" that gives you most screen real estate for DS emulation and four action buttons for $14.99; and finally the "Classic Faceplate", also $14.99 and offers four action buttons. So a full kit will cost anywhere between $29.98 and $34.98.

There's also decent repairability with it, which is a great feature and one I completely respect. PlayCase offer all of the small bits and parts to be purchased again for a few bucks should you want to tinker or fix your case in the future; from extra buttons to rubber bands to silicone pads, they'll sort you out should anything go wrong.

It's a fun way to add physical buttons to your device that can be snapped on and off easily. If you're willing to accept that you'll see printing lines and that some areas may lack strength, then this could be one to explore if you're looking for more comfortable emulator controls that include working shoulder buttons. It's certainly in a market of high competition too, seeing as the 8BITDO FlipPad has sold well, the GamesirTaco also, and then there's the GAMEBABY Case that does the same and is mass-produced in high-quality materials, though it has no back buttons.

It's worth noting that there is a sprinkling of Gen-AI amongst the website too, which isn't appreciated by the gaming community.

articles.description: GAME abre las reservas de Final Fantasy VII Revelation, la tercera entrega de la trilogía que llegará el 8 de abril de 2027, tanto de su edición estándar como de la Deluxe Edition para PS5, Switch 2 y Xbox.

h1: Final Fantasy VII Revelation ya se puede reservar en formato físico en GAME, incluyendo la impresionante Deluxe Edition para PS5, Switch 2 y Xbox

contentBlocks.text: El épico final de la trilogía de Final Fantasy VII Remake ya tiene fecha de lanzamiento. Será el 8 de abril de 2027 cuando Final Fantasy VII Revelation aterrice en PC y consolas, y en GAME se han anticipado a todos para abrir reservas de sus ediciones físicas. Final Fantasy VII Revelation ha presentado su increíble Deluxe Edition, que viene con el juego en formato físico y montones de extras, aunque es una pena que todas las versiones requieran de una descarga de contenido (es una tarjeta llave en Switch 2, por cierto).

Sea en su web o en cualquier tienda de la cadena, GAME anuncia que ya se puede reservar Final Fantasy VII Revelation para PS5, Nintendo Switch 2 y Xbox Series X, así que no os quedéis sin vuestra copia. Las reservas de FFVII Revelation ya están activas en GAME, y eso incluye la Deluxe Edition para PS5, Switch 2 y Xbox Final Fantasy VII Revelation tiene dos ediciones físicas distintas: por un lado está la Magic Card Edition, que incluye el juego en disco o cartucho junto a una carta promocional de Final Fantasy Showdown.

Esta edición se puede reservar por solo 3 euros para PS5, Switch 2 y Xbox, y su PVP recomendado es de 81,99 euros. El plato estrella es la Deluxe Edition, que trae el mismo contenido que la Magic Card Edition (el juego físico y la carta), pero con una presentación inmejorable y montones de extras en las tres plataformas.

Ya mismo se puede reservar por solo 5 euros. Su PVP recomendado es de 109,99 euros, y esto es todo lo que trae: Juego base con carátula reversible., Carta promocional "Final Fantasy Final Showdown"., Steelbook exclusiva., Libro de arte tapa dura., Banda sonora física en mini CD.

Ojo, porque las unidades de la Deluxe Edition son muy limitadas, así que corred a por ella porque tiene pinta de que se va a agotar muy pronto. También hay que decir que Final Fantasy VII Revelation no tiene edición física para PC. La de Xbox será compatible con el nuevo sistema de conversión de disco a digital (para que soporte Xbox Play Anywhere, juego en handhelds PC y el juego en la nube).

Las versiones de PS5 y Xbox Series X requieren de una descarga adicional para poder ejecutar el disco, mientras que la de Switch 2 viene en formato Game-Key Card y requiere de descargar todo el contenido desde Internet. Es el juego más grande de la consola hasta la fecha, con más de 130 GB de tamaño.

Final Fantasy VII Revelation pondrá el broche de oro a la trilogía de Cloud, Tifa, Barret y compañía a partir del 8 de abril de 2027 en PS5, Nintendo Switch 2, Xbox Series X|S y PC, pero solo las versiones para consolas tendrán ediciones físicas... ¡Que ya podéis reservar en GAME!

articles.title: Crítica de The Gentlemen temporada 2: Guy Ritchie regresa por sus fueros a Netflix
articles.description: Crítica de la segunda temporada de The Gentlemen: La serie, de estreno en Netflix el 3 de septiembre.

h1: Crítica de The Gentlemen temporada 2: Guy Ritchie regresa por sus fueros a Netflix

contentBlocks.text: Hemos visto los ocho episodios que componen la segunda temporada de The Gentlemen: La serie y que aterrizan en la plataforma Netflix hoy mismo. La buena nueva es que sigue despertando interés por la evolución de los personajes y que ya se ha renovado por una tercera temporada (el desenlace desde luego deja las cosas en un momento crítico), la no tan buena es que el listón sigue estando más bien bajo en lo que se refiere a la acción.

Ya comentamos a propósito de la primera temporada que se percibía como un producto menor respecto a la película. Ahora podemos asegurar que la línea es continuista en este sentido: no estamos ante el mejor Guy Ritchie. Sin embargo, ya nos hemos familiarizado con la galería de personajes y con el tono de la serie, que en esta ocasión apunta más alto, casi a hermanarse con El padrino y a abrazar el juego de contrastes entre los lujos, privilegios y supuesto acervo de la aristocracia y las familias de gánsteres, sicarios y personajes arribistas que amenazan con su caos el aparente orden que los primeros proponen... siempre a beneficio de sus abultados bolsillos.

Lo primero que hay que señalar es que la historia da muchas vueltas y a veces se recrea demasiado en subtramas que no van a ninguna parte. A este director venía acompañándole un sello autoral caracterizado por la mezcla de humor negro, diálogos elocuentes y secuencias de acción estilizadas pero, de un tiempo a esta parte, le cuesta encontrar el balance entre estos ingredientes y ofrece cada vez menos de lo que nos gusta.

Es decir que se recrea en el envoltorio pero mengua lo que mete dentro de él. A la serie The Gentlemen le falta algo de garra, que no violencia. Por otra parte, recala en los mismos problemas que ya vimos en la primera temporada: los personajes son bastante ásperos y al protagonista, Theo James, le falta registro interpretativo.

Da el tipo, sin lugar a dudas, y cumple tanto en el apartado de la acción como en el del estilismo, parte fundamental para un personaje adinerado y engreído como es el duque, pero su arco de evolución es la piedra de toque de toda la temporada y no alcanza a mostrar todo el rango de emociones que son necesarias para generar una respuesta empática en la audiencia.

Le falta carisma, no proyecta y se lo siguen comiendo con patatas otros intérpretes que tiene a su alrededor, desde Kaya Scodelario hasta Ray Winstone. Por lo demás la segunda temporada de The Gentlemen se detiene bastante en las vidas sentimentales de los protagonistas y se recrea en tensiones sexuales no resueltas a la par que estira una relación cuyo final es muy fácil adivinar.

El factor sorpresa juega en contra de una temporada que se percibe de bisagra y que, de alguna forma, se las apaña para dar un rodeo gigantesco para dejarnos en la rampa de salida de nuevo. Para eso aparta a uno de los personajes principales del foco dejándolo casi en el olvido para retomarlo al final.

En fin, a pesar de las muchas pegas que se le pueden poner a la serie, la puesta en escena sigue siendo impecable. Pocas pegas se le pueden poner al montaje y al trabajo del director en sí mismo. En verdad lo que más chirría es el guión en sí mismo, el diseño de los personajes, la cantidad de relleno de la historia y ciertos clichés que se cuelan incluso en los diálogos, a los que les falta chispa.

La sofisticación enfrentada al mundo criminal hace tiempo que dejó de ser original y definitivamente la serie sufre para mantener el interés en los personajes, que ni son tan verosímiles como para despertar una reflexión sobre la realidad ni tan fascinantes como para sustentar los soliloquios delirantes del personaje de Giancarlo Esposito.

selected.title: Prácticamente magia o El diablo viste de Prada muestran que la nostalgia es el más efectivo de los engaños
selected.description: La nostalgia nos hace creer que queremos pagar para ver segundas partes de películas que nos gustaron en su día, pero al salir del cine nos encontramos con una oscura realidad.

h1: Prácticamente magia o El diablo viste de Prada muestran que la nostalgia es el más efectivo de los engaños

contentBlocks.text: Estamos volviendo al pasado. Aunque, en honor a la verdad, el pasado es algo a lo que no paramos de volver porque nunca lo hemos soltado. La terrible trampa en la que nos hemos visto atrapadas se llama nostalgia. Si bien la nostalgia admite muchas formas y no se presenta de la misma manera para todo el mundo, porque al final es un estado condicionado por demasiados factores personales, la temporalidad acaba siendo un buen punto en común para el público.

Recuerdo cómo la película animada Red de Pixar pegó muy fuerte en 2022 porque nos hizo darnos cuenta de algo: La nostalgia de los 2020 ya no tiene que beber de manera necesaria de los años 80 porque la gente que creció en los 2000 es ahora mayor y empieza a recordar el pasado con ese cariño melancólico idéntico al que ha empujado a Hollywood durante décadas a rescatar el imaginario audiovisual de Steven Spielberg en sus largometrajes del siglo anterior.

Y, por eso mismo, este año hemos sido testigos de cómo han vuelto a las salas películas como Prácticamente magia (1998) o El diablo viste de Prada (2006) con sus respectivas secuelas un cuarto de lustro después. No es casualidad. Ahora es un buen momento para regresar a ellas, para atraer a una nueva generación a los cines.

Porque, y este es el elemento más importante del fenómeno, la nostalgia vende. ¿Segundas partes nunca fueron buenas? Si la primera te gustó, lo más seguro es que quieras ir a ver la segunda. No le vas a poner muchas pegas, te va a dar lo mismo de lo que trate, quién actué.

Tú conoces la base, el origen, y eso es lo único que te va a importar a la hora de lanzarte a pagar una entrada. Y, aun así, hay un giro en este juego del que todavía no eres consciente, pero que se te va a ir desvelando a medida que aceptes el engaño de la productora que quiso traer de vuelta tu querida película de los 2000.

En su día viste aquella cinta y tenía algo que te conquistó. Se quedó grabada en tu memoria, o perdida entre el resto de tus recuerdos, pero formó parte de tu vida en algún momento que fue mejor, porque el presente siempre empora frente a lo que proyectamos sobre lo que ya pasó.

Por eso, cuando anuncian una secuela algo se despierta en tu interior: la nostalgia. Ha pasado el tiempo, ¡cuanto más mejor! De repente tienes la genuina necesidad de querer saber qué pasó después: cómo habrá envejecido esa trama, qué más se podrá contar de esos personajes, ¿habrán evolucionado o se habrán estancado después de todos estos años?

La respuesta la tienes en dos nuevas horas de película que llegan para saciar tu FOMO por estas tres décadas olvidadas... Tan solo para que te des cuenta de que, al final, te acabas quedando con la primera cuando ya has pagado por la segunda. Y es que ha transcurrido demasiado tiempo desde que se lanzó la original.

Tú ya no eres esa chavala que en su día fue al cine a ver Prácticamente magia o El diablo viste de Prada, ahora eres una señora. Sí, te lo has pasado bien viendo la segunda parte, has recordado con cariño aquello que te gustaba entonces. Pero su historia nunca estará a la altura de la película que ya habías construido en tu cabeza sobre su posible retorno.

Eso que te hizo gracia hace 20 años o esas dinámicas que te llamaron la atención carecen de la chispa de la originalidad de entonces. Ahora ya no te gusta lo que te gustaba en aquel momento, su historia se siente como rescatar un barco que debía permanecer hundido para no corromperse fuera del océano que lo consumió.

La nostalgia te llama con una fuerza poderosa para que vuelvas a esos universos que conociste cuando todo era diferente, sin que esperes la decepción de encontrarte con que todo lo que te atraía de la secuela era lo que iba a hacer que no funcionase el reencuentro.
A veces es mejor no remover el pasado, dejarlo todo como está y recordarlo con cariño sin forzar su vuelta.

No es casualidad. Ahora es un buen momento para regresar a ellas, para atraer a una nueva generación a los cines.

Porque, y este es el elemento más importante del fenómeno, la nostalgia vende. ¿Segundas partes nunca fueron buenas? Si la primera te gustó, lo más seguro es que quieras ir a ver la segunda. No le vas a poner muchas pegas, te va a dar lo mismo de lo que trate, quién actué.

Tú conoces la base, el origen, y eso es lo único que te va a importar a la hora de lanzarte a pagar una entrada. Y, aun así, hay un giro en este juego del que todavía no eres consciente, pero que se te va a ir desvelando a medida que aceptes el engaño de la productora que quiso traer de vuelta tu querida película de los 2000.

En su día viste aquella cinta y tenía algo que te conquistó. Se quedó grabada en tu memoria, o perdida entre el resto de tus recuerdos, pero formó parte de tu vida en algún momento que fue mejor, porque el presente siempre empora frente a lo que proyectamos sobre lo que ya pasó.

Por eso, cuando anuncian una secuela algo se despierta en tu interior: la nostalgia. Ha pasado el tiempo, ¡cuanto más mejor! De repente tienes la genuina necesidad de querer saber qué pasó después: cómo habrá envejecido esa trama, qué más se podrá contar de esos personajes, ¿habrán evolucionado o se habrán estancado después de todos estos años?

La respuesta la tienes en dos nuevas horas de película que llegan para saciar tu FOMO por estas tres décadas olvidadas... Tan solo para que te des cuenta de que, al final, te acabas quedando con la primera cuando ya has pagado por la segunda. Y es que ha transcurrido demasiado tiempo desde que se lanzó la original.

Tú ya no eres esa chavala que en su día fue al cine a ver Prácticamente magia o El diablo viste de Prada, ahora eres una señora. Sí, te lo has pasado bien viendo la segunda parte, has recordado con cariño aquello que te gustaba entonces. Pero su historia nunca estará a la altura de la película que ya habías construido en tu cabeza sobre su posible retorno.

Eso que te hizo gracia hace 20 años o esas dinámicas que te llamaron la atención carecen de la chispa de la originalidad de entonces. Ahora ya no te gusta lo que te gustaba en aquel momento, su historia se siente como rescatar un barco que debía permanecer hundido para no corromperse fuera del océano que lo consumió.

La nostalgia te llama con una fuerza poderosa para que vuelvas a esos universos que conociste cuando todo era diferente, sin que esperes la decepción de encontrarte con que todo lo que te atraía de la secuela era lo que iba a hacer que no funcionase el reencuentro.

A veces es mejor no remover el pasado, dejarlo todo como está y recordarlo con cariño sin forzar su vuelta.

contentBlocks.text: A couple of days ago, Sony & LEGO announced the PlayStation set , featuring 1,911 bricks, releasing on October 4th and priced at £139.99/$179.99. It has gone down very well with most retro gamers (let's not talk about how it doesn't have 1,995 pieces), featuring two secret easter eggs on the inside which can be pulled out to display Ape Escape and Gran Turismo dioramas.

The LEGO set isn't out yet, but there's already something special in the works for this build: a mod kit from the makers of the BrickBoy . This kit will turn the LEGO PlayStation into a working games console thanks to an inserted Raspberry Pi Zero 2W offering PS1 Emulation, HDMI out and more.

The BrickBoy was an incredibly innovative piece of tech that transformed the GAME BOY into a working console that you built yourself; everything the team from Switzerland has learned from that first project is now going into developing a more advanced mod kit for the LEGO PlayStation, being named the BrickStation .

I spoke with the founder of BrickStation, Thomas Bertani, to get a better understanding of their upcoming product. It's clear that it's still in very early development; heck, they don't have the set yet, but they know exactly what they want to do, and how they're going to do it, so let me explain.

The components of the BrickStation will be assembled inside of an ABS, mould-injected "base"; this will contain the Raspberry Pi and all of the electronics, crammed into a build small enough to fit into the exact compartment that the Ape Escape diorama sits, allowing you to hopefully slide it into the console easily, perhaps not removing any bricks or pieces at all. Thomas said he wants this to be as close to "plug and play" as possible.

The Raspberry Pi internals will offer easy hook-up to an HDMI TV, offer wireless controller support, wired controller support via USB, the ability to use the Power On button on the LEGO PS1 and a "full-resolution, full-frame-rate" gaming experience. Thomas mentioned there will also be full compliance with regulations and certifications, which isn't something fan-made mod kits do, and can be dangerous, so it's clear Thomas and his team want this to be executed professionally and properly, which their BrickBoy did respectfully.

There's also a number of extra goodies and features that will be announced in the future that we cannot mention. You can follow BrickStation's journey at BrickStation.xyz , and you can likely expect the Kickstarter campaign to launch at the end of the month or around the official release of the LEGO set. As of now, we have no information regarding pricing or release date, but we're confident these guys will pull it off and no doubt they'll have a bunch of extra features and products to explore once the crowdfunding campaign goes live. We'll try our hardest to give you an early look at this, just like we did with the BrickBoy, so make sure to follow our free weekly newsletter to not miss out on that.

contentBlocks.text: by Todd Friedman | Sep 5, 2026 | 1990s , 2000s , Reviews

There are some arcade games that simply don’t need much introduction. ARKANOID is one of them. Originally released by Taito in 1986, the paddle-and-ball classic became one of the defining block-breaking games of the arcade era. Its 1987 sequel, ARKANOID: REVENGE OF DOH , took the basic formula and expanded it with new enemies, stage designs, power-ups, and challenges.

Now HAMSTER Corporation has brought ARKANOID: REVENGE OF DOH to Nintendo Switch 2 as part of its Arcade Archives 2 series. Rather than completely remake the game for modern audiences, HAMSTER takes a preservation-first approach, keeping the original arcade experience intact while adding modern features that make the game considerably more convenient to play today.
The result is one of those releases that understands exactly what makes an old arcade game special.
the ball, and advance through increasingly difficult stages.
The sequel adds considerably more variety to that formula. Blocks can move, regenerate, or behave differently, while enemies and obstacles make later stages much more challenging.
There is also a branching stage structure, allowing players to take different routes through the game.
Arcade Archives 2 Features
This is where HAMSTER’s Switch 2 release becomes more than simply playing an old game on new hardware.
The release includes several different ways to play, including Original Mode, Hi Score Mode, Caravan Mode, and Time Attack Mode.
Time Attack is particularly interesting because it changes the objective. Instead of concentrating exclusively on score, you’re trying to complete the game as quickly as possible.
There are also save features, online rankings, rewind functionality, and rapid-fire options.
These additions don’t fundamentally change REVENGE OF DOH . Instead, they give modern players different ways to enjoy the original game.
That is exactly the approach I want to see from a classic-game collection.
At around the $10 price point, this is an easy recommendation for classic arcade fans.
The value proposition is somewhat different for players who aren’t interested in arcade history.
You’re essentially buying a faithful recreation of a game that is nearly four decades old, rather than a brand-new Switch 2 production.
But for players who appreciate classic arcade gaming, that’s precisely the appeal.
HAMSTER has preserved the original game while adding features that make it considerably easier to enjoy on modern hardware.

h2: The Interface Details That Made Computer Solitaire Feel Timeless

contentBlocks.text: The Interface Details That Made Computer Solitaire Feel Timeless
Posted by Retromash
in Misc
Tagged with

Computer solitaire became memorable because it made a new machine feel understandable. A modern round on PlaySolitaire still uses the same essential visual language: a deck, clear columns, visible suits and cards that respond directly to the player. The technology around the game has changed dramatically, but the interaction remains immediate. That is why solitaire belongs in any conversation about the everyday design of classic computer games.

A deck became a lesson in mouse movement When Solitaire arrived with Windows 3.0 in 1990, many home computer users were still becoming comfortable with a mouse. Moving cards from one pile to another gave drag and drop a purpose that was easy to grasp. The player did not need to understand files, menus or commands. They only needed to recognise a card and place it where the rules allowed.

That was clever interface design disguised as a familiar pastime. The action on screen matched an action people already understood from the physical world. A card could be selected, moved and released. If the destination was wrong, the game refused the move. The feedback was simple and immediate.

The desktop game that needed little explanation Many early computer games had to teach players a new language. They introduced unfamiliar controls, icons and objectives at the same time. Solitaire avoided much of that work because the deck already carried meaning.

Red and black suits were easy to distinguish. Ordered columns showed progress. Empty spaces suggested possibility. The stock pile invited a click. Even a player who did not know every rule could experiment and learn from the response.

This made the game unusually approachable. It felt like software, but it did not feel technical. That balance helped it become part of the everyday computer rather than a special activity reserved for dedicated players.

Small interface choices built trust Classic solitaire interfaces were rarely spectacular. Their strength came from consistency. Cards stayed where they were placed. Legal moves behaved predictably. A completed sequence created a visible sense of order.

Those details built trust between the player and the machine. The computer was not hiding the rules or asking for a complicated input. It was maintaining the table, enforcing the structure and keeping score.

The same principle still matters in modern design. A good interface should make the next action feel obvious without making the result automatic. Solitaire achieves this with very little visual clutter. The player can see the problem, but solving it still requires attention.

Nostalgia is visual, but usability keeps it alive The green felt background and pixel card backs are powerful nostalgic images. They recall family computers, office breaks and the particular sound of a mouse button. Yet nostalgia alone does not explain why the game survives.

People return because the underlying interaction remains useful. A round starts quickly. Progress is visible. Failure is understandable. A new attempt creates a different arrangement without requiring a tutorial.

This is also why many attempts to modernise classic games go too far. Extra animations, reward systems and crowded menus can obscure the quality that made the original work. Solitaire does not need to pretend to be bigger than it is. Its modest scale is part of the appeal.

The browser is the new family computer The family computer once gathered software in a single physical place. Today, the browser performs a similar role across laptops, tablets and phones. It provides a common surface where a familiar game can appear without installation or a long setup process.

That shift changes access, but not the core experience. A card still needs a clear destination. A sequence still needs to be read. The player still chooses between an immediate move and a more patient plan.

Browser play also preserves another old habit: using a simple game as a boundary between tasks. One round can mark the end of work, fill a short wait or provide a calm reset before returning to something more demanding.

Why the old rhythm survives Computer solitaire lasts because its rhythm was never tied to one machine. It begins with disorder, asks for careful attention and rewards the gradual creation of structure. The interface supports that rhythm without getting in the way.

That is a useful lesson from classic software. Technology becomes memorable when it gives people a clear action, a reliable response and enough space to make their own decisions. Solitaire did that on the early desktop, and it continues to do it in the browser today.

Now, a well-known retro-gaming YouTuber known as Ryan Retro has spent the last few months developing his very own Android frontend for emulators, again with a focus on the physical aspect of digital collecting. This seems to be a trend after Sony's big announcement of stopping the production of physical games.

Ryan is calling this frontend "Jump", conveniently named because of the application's ease of jumping to certain games in your collection. Ryan wants it to be a simple yet effective way to organise your ROM library using its box art, allowing you to resize, readjust and move around the collection in a way that's natural to you; heck, you even choose case view, which makes your cartridges look like they're in an old 2000s storage case surrounded by foam and your discs look like they're in a transparent sleeve.

There's a whole lot of customisations in here that make it easy for you to find a display that suits your needs; you can choose from Grid, Shelf, Tower and Case, and each allows you to change between light and dark themes, even going as far as adding a wooden shelf mode too, to keep things nostalgic. These views are kept when searching for your games using the keyboard too.

One of the craziest features though, is the fact that Ryan has built his own scraping service for box art and disc/cartidge art, so you don't have to pair this with any external app or service such as ScreenScraper, you literally press "download it for me" and Jump will automatically find, download and update your ROM library with box art images and cartridge/disc art so that your collection is organised visually straight after installing it. That's incredible, and kudos to Ryan for making it incredibly fluid. Just make sure your ROM files are named exactly the same as the game title for this to work smoothly.

You can also add multiple folders to a specific console, which is not typical of frontends, allowing you to take advantage of the internal and external storage at the same time. This syncs up your entire library wherever it may be. It works with an array of Android-based retro handhelds, and even dual-screen ones too such as the AYN Thor.

This frontend is locked behind a Patreon paywall , which is typical of indie-made frontends these days, so to get hold of it you'll have to throw Ryan a few bucks to get access to this frontend on Android. You'll also get updates and newer updates as the months go on without having to keep paying, so $3 will get you this app and its continued updates, which is awesome.

h1: Atari and Vice Beer Introduce New Beer Collection

contentBlocks.text: by Old School Gamer | Sep 5, 2026 | 1980s , 1990s , Press Release
ATARI AND VICE BEER INTRODUCE NEW BEER COLLECTION
The four-pack of Atari-themed beer is available now.

September 5, 2026 – Atari and Vice Beer are celebrating a new licensing collaboration during PAX West in Seattle. Vancouver, Washington-based Vice Beer has released a four-pack of Atari-themed 16 oz. beers, including One-Button Joystick WC IPA, Gemstone Sour, Sunken Treasure and Original Bug Battle Hazy IPA. The four-packs can be purchased online via atari.com or at shop.tavour.com .

“I remember the thrill of walking into an arcade with a pocket full of quarters, and that is how I feel sharing these hand-crafted, Atari-themed beers with fans,” said Michael Perozzo, co-founder of Vice Beer. “There is something for everyone in this collection, and the artwork is satisfyingly retro.”
The four-beer collection includes:

One-Button Joystick – 1x 16oz can – WCIPA – 6.9% ABV Featuring the absolutely iconic controller of the Atari 2600, Vice and Atari opted for a suitable craft classic for One-Button Joystick — a West Coast IPA. The crushable Westie starts with a Pilsner malt base for a crisp sip that’ll keep you quenched as you blast asteroid after asteroid. It is hopped with Columbus Cryo, Strata, Idaho 7, Citra, Mosaic Cryo, and Quantum Mosaic, culminating in a sip as mind blowing as being able to play Asteroids … in your house! Which in the ‘80s was pretty exciting!

Expect bright mango and grapefruit to lead each dynamic swig with hints of tropical fruit and mixed berry flowing underneath. Nuances of orange peel and piney resin should bring a refreshing balance that’ll have you diving back in for another sip like you’re trying to set a high score!

Original Bug Battle – 1x 16oz can – NEIPA – 6.4% ABV Look for luscious mandarin and peach to weave like a Centipede through notes of pineapple and strawberry on every pillowy swig. Zesty lime and white grape tones ought to crawl underneath with just enough peppery bitterness on the finish to balance all that nectar.

To craft this IPA, the team brewed a soft base with Pilsner malt, flaked oat, and torrified wheat. Then they blasted it with Nelson, Motueka, Strata, Citra Cryo, Mosaic Cryo, and Quantum Galaxy for surges of straight nectar. It all makes for Haze so satisfying, you’ll be after every last drop like they’re segments of a centipede that need destroying!

Gemstone Sour – 1x 16oz can – Fruited Sour – 5% ABV Like Bentley Bear working his way through colorful fortresses in search of gems in the arcade classic Crystal Castles, you’ll find yourself happily lost in a maze of jammy bramble fruit and succulent citrus with every swig of this Sour. Imagine an extra tangy take on a berry lemonade and you have a decent idea what’s in store!
This gem is brewed with castle-sized quantities of actual raspberries and lemons. Paired with a tart Sour Ale base, it makes for an invigorating swig that’ll keep you going game after game!

Sunken Treasure – 1x 16oz can – Imperial Stout – 8% ABV For this stunner, Vice teamed up with Nightdive Studios — a game studio and part of the Atari family with an emphasis on retro video game preservation and restoration. That’s fitting, since once you get a taste of this Stout, you’ll probably be looking to preserve every last bit all for yourself!

Especially with all the sumptuous s’mores flavors brimming out of each quaff courtesy of toasted marshmallows, graham crackers, and cacao nibs. Your average campfire treat doesn’t come with delectable espresso tones and hints of caramel from a bold malty base. Oh, and an 8% ABV!

“Nightdive has always been about celebrating the games and experiences that made us fall in love with this medium, and there’s something special about seeing that passion extend beyond the screen,” said Stephen Kick, studio head at Nightdive. “Collaborating with Vice Beer and Atari on Sunken Treasure was a fun way to bring a little piece of that history into the real world. Games are meant to be shared, remembered and enjoyed — and in this case, so is the beer.”

selected.title: Final Fantasy VII Revelation ya se puede reservar en formato físico en GAME, incluyendo la impresionante Deluxe Edition para PS5, Switch 2 y Xbox
selected.description: GAME abre las reservas de Final Fantasy VII Revelation, la tercera entrega de la trilogía que llegará el 8 de abril de 2027, tanto de su edición estándar como de la Deluxe Edition para PS5, Switch 2 y Xbox.

h1: Final Fantasy VII Revelation ya se puede reservar en formato físico en GAME, incluyendo la impresionante Deluxe Edition para PS5, Switch 2 y Xbox

contentBlocks.text: El épico final de la trilogía de Final Fantasy VII Remake ya tiene fecha de lanzamiento. Será el 8 de abril de 2027 cuando Final Fantasy VII Revelation aterrice en PC y consolas, y en GAME se han anticipado a todos para abrir reservas de sus ediciones físicas. Final Fantasy VII Revelation ha presentado su increíble Deluxe Edition, que viene con el juego en formato físico y montones de extras, aunque es una pena que todas las versiones requieran de una descarga de contenido (es una tarjeta llave en Switch 2, por cierto).

Sea en su web o en cualquier tienda de la cadena, GAME anuncia que ya se puede reservar Final Fantasy VII Revelation para PS5, Nintendo Switch 2 y Xbox Series X, así que no os quedéis sin vuestra copia. Las reservas de FFVII Revelation ya están activas en GAME, y eso incluye la Deluxe Edition para PS5, Switch 2 y Xbox Final Fantasy VII Revelation tiene dos ediciones físicas distintas: por un lado está la Magic Card Edition, que incluye el juego en disco o cartucho junto a una carta promocional de Final Fantasy Showdown.

Esta edición se puede reservar por solo 3 euros para PS5, Switch 2 y Xbox, y su PVP recomendado es de 81,99 euros. El plato estrella es la Deluxe Edition, que trae el mismo contenido que la Magic Card Edition (el juego físico y la carta), pero con una presentación inmejorable y montones de extras en las tres plataformas.

Ya mismo se puede reservar por solo 5 euros. Su PVP recomendado es de 109,99 euros, y esto es todo lo que trae: Juego base con carátula reversible., Carta promocional "Final Fantasy Final Showdown"., Steelbook exclusiva., Libro de arte tapa dura., Banda sonora física en mini CD.

Ojo, porque las unidades de la Deluxe Edition son muy limitadas, así que corred a por ella porque tiene pinta de que se va a agotar muy pronto. También hay que decir que Final Fantasy VII Revelation no tiene edición física para PC. La de Xbox será compatible con el nuevo sistema de conversión de disco a digital (para que soporte Xbox Play Anywhere, juego en handhelds PC y el juego en la nube).

Las versiones de PS5 y Xbox Series X requieren de una descarga adicional para poder ejecutar el disco, mientras que la de Switch 2 viene en formato Game-Key Card y requiere de descargar todo el contenido desde Internet. Es el juego más grande de la consola hasta la fecha, con más de 130 GB de tamaño.

Final Fantasy VII Revelation pondrá el broche de oro a la trilogía de Cloud, Tifa, Barret y compañía a partir del 8 de abril de 2027 en PS5, Nintendo Switch 2, Xbox Series X|S y PC, pero solo las versiones para consolas tendrán ediciones físicas... ¡Que ya podéis reservar en GAME!

h1: Hyperkin Bring Modern Power To Retro Consoles With New USB-C Charging System Range

contentBlocks.text: I'm a big fan of Hyperkin and their mission to make it even easier to play the consoles of yesteryear, especially when it comes to providing a simple power solution that works with all of your old consoles. Enter Shockline, their new range of cables and adapters that swap out the myriad of cables and plugs you used to use for simple USB-C solutions, meaning you can power them all from a USB-C bank or just use one plug socket for swapping between machines.
The ShockLine range is out right now, with both charging cable kits and power supply kits available to purchase. In terms of home consoles, you can purchase:
And in the handhelds range:
Built with flexible, kink-resistant cabling and (on the handheld kits) built-in overcharge protection, so your system stays powered without the wear and tear that comes with old, worn-out originals.

The sets come with the adapters and power supply kits mentioned, as well as a 6-foot USB-C cable so you can place your consoles effectively without having to tower them on top of each other - we've worked with some companies that send the smallest USB cables known to gaming kind with their products, so this is a nice feature.

Honestly, they're priced really well too. The power supply kits for the N64, GameCube, and Retro Console group cost $24.99, which is about £18.50. The charging cable kits cost $19.99, which is around £14.79. For power solutions that remove the need for tonnes of bulky wires behind your TV, I think that's a great price, especially because power cords end up getting lost or damaged over the years too. The NES is 40 years old, for crying out loud - I wouldn't be surprised if most of the wires out there are frayed or held together with tape!
Head to Hyperkin for more information!

selected.title: Crítica de The Gentlemen temporada 2: Guy Ritchie regresa por sus fueros a Netflix
selected.description: Crítica de la segunda temporada de The Gentlemen: La serie, de estreno en Netflix el 3 de septiembre.

h1: Crítica de The Gentlemen temporada 2: Guy Ritchie regresa por sus fueros a Netflix

contentBlocks.text: Hemos visto los ocho episodios que componen la segunda temporada de The Gentlemen: La serie y que aterrizan en la plataforma Netflix hoy mismo. La buena nueva es que sigue despertando interés por la evolución de los personajes y que ya se ha renovado por una tercera temporada (el desenlace desde luego deja las cosas en un momento crítico), la no tan buena es que el listón sigue estando más bien bajo en lo que se refiere a la acción.

Ya comentamos a propósito de la primera temporada que se percibía como un producto menor respecto a la película. Ahora podemos asegurar que la línea es continuista en este sentido: no estamos ante el mejor Guy Ritchie. Sin embargo, ya nos hemos familiarizado con la galería de personajes y con el tono de la serie, que en esta ocasión apunta más alto, casi a hermanarse con El padrino y a abrazar el juego de contrastes entre los lujos, privilegios y supuesto acervo de la aristocracia y las familias de gánsteres, sicarios y personajes arribistas que amenazan con su caos el aparente orden que los primeros proponen... siempre a beneficio de sus abultados bolsillos.

Lo primero que hay que señalar es que la historia da muchas vueltas y a veces se recrea demasiado en subtramas que no van a ninguna parte. A este director venía acompañándole un sello autoral caracterizado por la mezcla de humor negro, diálogos elocuentes y secuencias de acción estilizadas pero, de un tiempo a esta parte, le cuesta encontrar el balance entre estos ingredientes y ofrece cada vez menos de lo que nos gusta.

Es decir que se recrea en el envoltorio pero mengua lo que mete dentro de él. A la serie The Gentlemen le falta algo de garra, que no violencia. Por otra parte, recala en los mismos problemas que ya vimos en la primera temporada: los personajes son bastante ásperos y al protagonista, Theo James, le falta registro interpretativo.

Da el tipo, sin lugar a dudas, y cumple tanto en el apartado de la acción como en el del estilismo, parte fundamental para un personaje adinerado y engreído como es el duque, pero su arco de evolución es la piedra de toque de toda la temporada y no alcanza a mostrar todo el rango de emociones que son necesarias para generar una respuesta empática en la audiencia.

Le falta carisma, no proyecta y se lo siguen comiendo con patatas otros intérpretes que tiene a su alrededor, desde Kaya Scodelario hasta Ray Winstone. Por lo demás la segunda temporada de The Gentlemen se detiene bastante en las vidas sentimentales de los protagonistas y se recrea en tensiones sexuales no resueltas a la par que estira una relación cuyo final es muy fácil adivinar.

El factor sorpresa juega en contra de una temporada que se percibe de bisagra y que, de alguna forma, se las apaña para dar un rodeo gigantesco para dejarnos en la rampa de salida de nuevo. Para eso aparta a uno de los personajes principales del foco dejándolo casi en el olvido para retomarlo al final.

En fin, a pesar de las muchas pegas que se le pueden poner a la serie, la puesta en escena sigue siendo impecable. Pocas pegas se le pueden poner al montaje y al trabajo del director en sí mismo. En verdad lo que más chirría es el guión en sí mismo, el diseño de los personajes, la cantidad de relleno de la historia y ciertos clichés que se cuelan incluso en los diálogos, a los que les falta chispa.

La sofisticación enfrentada al mundo criminal hace tiempo que dejó de ser original y definitivamente la serie sufre para mantener el interés en los personajes, que ni son tan verosímiles como para despertar una reflexión sobre la realidad ni tan fascinantes como para sustentar los soliloquios delirantes del personaje de Giancarlo Esposito.

Hemos visto los ocho episodios que componen la segunda temporada de The Gentlemen: La serie y que aterrizan en la plataforma Netflix hoy mismo. La buena nueva es que sigue despertando interés por la evolución de los personajes y que ya se ha renovado por una tercera temporada (el desenlace desde luego deja las cosas en un momento crítico), la no tan buena es que el listón sigue estando más bien bajo en lo que se refiere a la acción.

Ya comentamos a propósito de la primera temporada que se percibía como un producto menor respecto a la película. Ahora podemos asegurar que la línea es continuista en este sentido: no estamos ante el mejor Guy Ritchie. Sin embargo, ya nos hemos familiarizado con la galería de personajes y con el tono de la serie, que en esta ocasión apunta más alto, casi a hermanarse con El padrino y a abrazar el juego de contrastes entre los lujos, privilegios y supuesto acervo de la aristocracia y las familias de gánsteres, sicarios y personajes arribistas que amenazan con su caos el aparente orden que los primeros proponen... siempre a beneficio de sus abultados bolsillos.

Lo primero que hay que señalar es que la historia da muchas vueltas y a veces se recrea demasiado en subtramas que no van a ninguna parte. A este director venía acompañándole un sello autoral caracterizado por la mezcla de humor negro, diálogos elocuentes y secuencias de acción estilizadas pero, de un tiempo a esta parte, le cuesta encontrar el balance entre estos ingredientes y ofrece cada vez menos de lo que nos gusta.

Es decir que se recrea en el envoltorio pero mengua lo que mete dentro de él. A la serie The Gentlemen le falta algo de garra, que no violencia. Por otra parte, recala en los mismos problemas que ya vimos en la primera temporada: los personajes son bastante ásperos y al protagonista, Theo James, le falta registro interpretativo.

Da el tipo, sin lugar a dudas, y cumple tanto en el apartado de la acción como en el del estilismo, parte fundamental para un personaje adinerado y engreído como es el duque, pero su arco de evolución es la piedra de toque de toda la temporada y no alcanza a mostrar todo el rango de emociones que son necesarias para generar una respuesta empática en la audiencia.

Le falta carisma, no proyecta y se lo siguen comiendo con patatas otros intérpretes que tiene a su alrededor, desde Kaya Scodelario hasta Ray Winstone. Por lo demás la segunda temporada de The Gentlemen se detiene bastante en las vidas sentimentales de los protagonistas y se recrea en tensiones sexuales no resueltas a la par que estira una relación cuyo final es muy fácil adivinar.

El factor sorpresa juega en contra de una temporada que se percibe de bisagra y que, de alguna forma, se las apaña para dar un rodeo gigantesco para dejarnos en la rampa de salida de nuevo. Para eso aparta a uno de los personajes principales del foco dejándolo casi en el olvido para retomarlo al final.

En fin, a pesar de las muchas pegas que se le pueden poner a la serie, la puesta en escena sigue siendo impecable. Pocas pegas se le pueden poner al montaje y al trabajo del director en sí mismo. En verdad lo que más chirría es el guión en sí mismo, el diseño de los personajes, la cantidad de relleno de la historia y ciertos clichés que se cuelan incluso en los diálogos, a los que les falta chispa.

La sofisticación enfrentada al mundo criminal hace tiempo que dejó de ser original y definitivamente la serie sufre para mantener el interés en los personajes, que ni son tan verosímiles como para despertar una reflexión sobre la realidad ni tan fascinantes como para sustentar los soliloquios delirantes del personaje de Giancarlo Esposito.

contentBlocks.text: This is a product I have been following for a long time, and I have even been in discussions with their team regarding review samples, but I'll be completely honest: I still don't know how to feel about this product, and I'll explain why. But I know some of our Retro Dodo readers will find this thing interesting, so I want to put a spotlight on it, seeing as it's now officially available to purchase and I know the owner behind it has been hard at work making this a real thing.

The PlayCase is a new phone case for iPhone (and the Samsung Galaxy S26) that adds physical buttons which pair with a range of emulators such as Delta, RetroArch, and more, similar to the GAMEBABY case that we have reviewed in the past.

What's cool is that the controller part of the case is removable and is stored on the back of the case over the cameras; this can then be snapped off and used on the front of the iPhone as buttons. Keen eyes will also see that this has triggers too, which are located on the back. I am still uncertain how these work because the "learn more" button under the triggers part of the website doesn't work, but I believe it uses rubber bands that wrap around the case internally to activate on-screen presses.

My issue here lies in the manufacturing process. This is 3D printed, and from previous experience, these types of 3D printed products feel scratchy, flakey, are flimsy, and lack strength in the overall build, which is needed in a case that's going to protect a $1,000+ smartphone. However, I have yet to try it in person; this is just something I have experience with, as I own and operate GAMENOOK , a collectable accessory company that manufactures plastic products made from 100% recycled plastic handpressed into aluminium moulds. We tried 3D printing, but it lacked strength and overall quality, and I fear this is the same.

If you don't mind that, and are a fan of 3D-printed products like this, then let me tell you more about this quirky device. The main product is the "PlayCase Case", which surrounds your iPhone; this costs $19.99, and you then pair it with a "Faceplate". You have three to choose from: a "Handheld Faceplate" costing $9.99 that features a DPAD and two action buttons; there's a "Dual Screen Faceplate" that gives you most screen real estate for DS emulation and four action buttons for $14.99; and finally the "Classic Faceplate", also $14.99 and offers four action buttons. So a full kit will cost anywhere between $29.98 and $34.98.

There's also decent repairability with it, which is a great feature and one I completely respect. PlayCase offer all of the small bits and parts to be purchased again for a few bucks should you want to tinker or fix your case in the future; from extra buttons to rubber bands to silicone pads, they'll sort you out should anything go wrong.

It's a fun way to add physical buttons to your device that can be snapped on and off easily. If you're willing to accept that you'll see printing lines and that some areas may lack strength, then this could be one to explore if you're looking for more comfortable emulator controls that include working shoulder buttons. It's certainly in a market of high competition too, seeing as the 8BITDO FlipPad has sold well, the GamesirTaco also, and then there's the GAMEBABY Case that does the same and is mass-produced in high-quality materials, though it has no back buttons.
It's worth noting that there is a sprinkling of Gen-AI amongst the website too, which isn't appreciated by the gaming community.
